title: Men and beasts at the beginning
source_text: Εἶτα λέγει πρὸς τὸ τῶν αἰσθανομένων τῆς ἑαυτῶν ὑπεροχῆς ἀνθρώπων γένος. ἣν ὑπερέχει τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων. ὅτι πρὸς ὅ ὑμεῖς φατε, ὡς ὁ θεὸς ἡμῖν δέδωκεν αἱρεῖν τὰ θηρία δύνασθαι καὶ καταχρήσασθαι, ἐροῦμεν ὅτι ὡς εἰκὸς. πρὶν πόλεις εἶναι καὶ τέχνας καὶ τοιαύτας ἐπιμιξίας καὶ ὅπλα καὶ δίκτυα. ἄνθρωποι μὲν ὑπὸ θηρίων ἡρπάζοντο καὶ ἠσθίοντο. θηρία δ᾿ ὑπ᾿ ἀνθρώπων ἥκιστα ἡλίσκετο. ὅρα δὲ πρὸς ταῦτα ὅτι, εἰ καὶ αἱροῦσιν ἄνθρωποι θηρία καὶ θηρία ἀνθρώπους ἁρπάζει. πολλή ἐστι διαφορὰ τῶν συνέσει κρατούντων παρὰ τὰ ἀγριότητι καὶ ὠμότητι περιγινόμενα τῶν οὐ χρωμένων τῇ συνέσει πρὸς τὸ μηδὲν ὑπὸ θηρίων παθεῖν. τὸ δὲ πρὶν πόλεις εἶναι καὶ τέχνας καὶ τοιαύτας ἐπιμιξίας ἐπιλελησμένου οἶμαι εἶναι ὧν ἀνωτέρω προεῖπεν. ὡς ἀγενήτου ὄντος τοῦ κόσμου καὶ ἀφθάρτου. καὶ μόνων τῶν ἐπὶ γῆς κατακλυσμοὺς καὶ ἐκπυρώσεις πασχόντων, καὶ οὐ πάντων ἅμα τούτοις περιπιπτόντων. ὡς οὐκ ἔστιν οὖν τοῖς ἀγένητον ὑφισταμένοις τὸν κόσμον ἀρχὴν αὐτοῦ εἰπεῖν. οὕτως οὐδὲ χρόνον. ὅτ᾿ οὐδαμῶς ἦσαν πόλεις οὐδὲ τέχναι πω εὕρηντο. ἀλλ᾿ ἔστω καὶ ταῦτα ἡμῖν μὲν συνᾳδόντως αὐτῷ συγχωρεῖν αὐτῷ δὲ καὶ τοῖς ἀνωτέρω ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ λελεγμένοις οὐκέτι· τί οὖν τοῦτο πρὸς τὸ πάντως κατ᾿ ἀρχὰς τοὺς μὲν ἀνθρώπους ὑπὸ θηρίων ἁρπάζεσθαι καὶ ἐσθίεσθαι. μηκέτι δὲ τὰ θηρία ὑπ᾿ ἀνθρώπων ἁλίσκεσθαι; εἴπερ γὰρ κατὰ πρόνοιαν ὁ κόσμος γεγένηται, καὶ θεὸς ἐφέστηκε τοῖς ὅλοις, ἀναγκαῖον ἦν τὰ ζώπυρα τοῦ γένους τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀρξάμενα ὑπό τινα γεγονέναι φρουρὰν τὴν ἀπὸ κρειττόνων. ὥστε κατ᾿ ἀρχὰς ἐπιμιξίαν γεγονέναι τῆς θείας φύσεως πρὸς τοὺς ἀνθρώπους. ἅπερ καὶ ὁ Ἀσκραῖος ποιητὴς ἐννοῶν εἶπε· ξυναὶ γὰρ τότε δαῖτες ἔσαν, ξυνοὶ δὲ θόωκοι ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι καταθνητοῖς τ᾿ ἀνθρώποις.
pass_a_gloss: Then he says (λέγω) to the race (γένος) of men who perceive (αἰσθάνομαι) their own superiority (ὑπεροχή), by which they excel (ὑπερέχω) the irrational animals (ἄλογα ζῷα), [Celsus:] 'toward what you say, that God has given us to be able to catch (αἱρέω) the beasts (θηρίον) and use them fully (καταχράομαι), we will say that, as is likely (ὡς εἰκός), before there were cities (πόλις) and arts (τέχνη) and such minglings/social dealings (ἐπιμιξία) and weapons (ὅπλον) and nets (δίκτυον), men were snatched (ἁρπάζω) and eaten (ἐσθίω) by beasts, but beasts were least of all (ἥκιστα) caught (ἁλίσκομαι) by men.' See (ὁράω) toward these things that, even if men catch beasts and beasts snatch men, there is much difference (διαφορά) between those prevailing (κρατέω) by understanding (σύνεσις) and the things that get the better (περιγίνομαι) by wildness (ἀγριότης) and rawness/cruelty (ὠμότης) of those not using understanding toward suffering (πάσχω) nothing from beasts. The 'before there were cities and arts and such minglings' is, I think (οἶμαι), of one having forgotten (ἐπιλανθάνομαι) what he said above (ἀνωτέρω): that the world (κόσμος) is unbegotten (ἀγένητος) and incorruptible (ἄφθαρτος), and only things on earth suffer floods (κατακλυσμός) and conflagrations (ἐκπύρωσις), and not all fall into (περιπίπτω) these at once (ἅμα). As then it is not possible for those positing (ὑφίστημι) the world unbegotten to speak of a beginning (ἀρχή) of it, so neither a time (χρόνος) when there were in no way cities nor arts yet had been found (εὑρίσκω). But let it be (ἔστω) that we concede (συγχωρέω) these things to him, consistently (συνᾳδόντως) for us, but for him and for what was said above by him no longer (οὐκέτι). What then is this toward the [claim] that altogether (πάντως) at the beginnings (κατ᾿ ἀρχάς) men were snatched and eaten by beasts, but no longer (μηκέτι) the beasts were caught by men? For if (εἴπερ) the world came to be according to providence (πρόνοια), and God presides over (ἐφίστημι) the whole (τὰ ὅλα), it was necessary (ἀναγκαῖον) that the embers/live sparks (ζώπυρα) of the race of men, having begun, came to be under some guard (φρουρά) from stronger/better ones (κρείττονες), so that at the beginnings there came to be a mingling/intercourse (ἐπιμιξία) of the divine nature (θεία φύσις) toward men. Which things also the Ascraean poet (Ἀσκραῖος ποιητής) considering (ἐννοέω) said: 'for common (ξυνός) then were feasts (δαίς), and common the seats (θόωκος), for immortal gods and mortal men.'
pass_b_english: Next, addressing the race of men who perceive their own superiority over the irrational animals, he says: “As for what you say, that God has given us the power to catch wild beasts and make use of them, we shall reply that, in all likelihood, before there were cities and arts and such ways of living together, and weapons and nets, men were carried off and eaten by wild beasts, while wild beasts were very seldom caught by men.”

Observe, in answer to this, that even if men catch wild beasts and wild beasts carry off men, there is a great difference between those who prevail by understanding and the beasts that get the better, by savagery and cruelty, of men who do not use their understanding to keep from suffering anything at the hands of beasts.

And the words “before there were cities and arts and such ways of living together” come, I think, from a man who has forgotten what he said earlier: that the world is unbegotten and indestructible, and that only the things on earth suffer floods and conflagrations, and that not all of them meet with these at once. Just as those who hold that the world is unbegotten cannot speak of its beginning, so neither can they speak of a time when there were no cities at all and the arts had not yet been discovered.

But let us grant him this too; it agrees with our own views, though no longer with his, or with what he said earlier. What has this to do with the claim that at the beginning men were certainly carried off and eaten by wild beasts, while the beasts were not caught by men? For if the world came into being by providence, and God presides over the universe, the first sparks of the human race, when it began, must have come under some protection from higher beings, so that at the beginning there was fellowship between the divine nature and men. The poet of Ascra had this in mind when he said: “For then the feasts were shared, and the seats were shared, by immortal gods and mortal men” (Hesiod, Catalogue of Women, fragment 1.6–7).

choices.choice: Removed comma so 'men who perceive their own superiority' stays restrictive as in the Greek
Hesiod lines: dropped the inverted 'shared the seats' word order; citation Catalogue of Women fr. 1.6-7 confirmed (Origen is the source of this fragment)

Celsus's words (from ὡς εἰκός to ἡλίσκετο) are direct speech in the Greek and are in quotation marks. ἐπιμιξίαι rendered 'ways of living together' (social dealings, intercourse); the same word in the last sentence (ἐπιμιξία τῆς θείας φύσεως) rendered 'fellowship'. 'What he said earlier' points back to Celsus's claims on the unbegotten world and partial floods and conflagrations (cited by Origen at 1.19–20 and 4.11). συνᾳδόντως αὐτῷ: I take αὐτῷ as the dative with συγχωρεῖν ('grant him') and the contrast as 'consistent for us, no longer for him'; the syntax is compressed. μηκέτι in the restated claim is rendered simply 'not' (literally 'no longer'); Celsus himself said ἥκιστα, 'very seldom'. ζώπυρα ('embers, live sparks') rendered 'first sparks'. The Hesiod lines are from the Catalogue of Women, fragment 1.6–7 in Merkelbach–West; 'the poet of Ascra' is Hesiod. No Scripture quoted or alluded to.
